title: [Bug][KVOffload] PD Multi Tier discards parked KV after a fixed 60s, so a queued consumer recomputes
body:
### Your current environment

vLLM `main` (nightly `5a4c8d99`), plus #52912 applied. Two instances,
prefill and decode, each running `OffloadingConnector` with
`TieringOffloadingSpec` (CPU primary + `p2p` secondary tier).

### Describe the bug

A PD Multi Tier producer discards stored KV 60 s after `submit_store` when no
`FetchMsg` has bound the `kv_request_id` yet, so a consumer whose fetch is
issued later finds nothing, burns its own 30 s load deadline, and recomputes
the prompt.

`_UNBOUND_STORE_TIMEOUT_S = 60.0` (`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/manager.py`)
is a fixed timer counted from store time. Nothing ties it to whether the
consumer's request still exists or is merely queued behind other work, so the
reap can fire while the request it belongs to is perfectly alive. When the
late fetch arrives, the consumer waits out `_LOAD_TIMEOUT_S = 30.0`
(`.../p2p/session/client.py`) before falling back to recompute.

This is separate from #52808 and is not addressed by #52912; that fix makes a
warm producer cascade its blocks, this is about how long those blocks survive
while the peer has not asked for them yet.

Reproduced with two vLLM instances and three curls - no router, no proxy, no
scheduler involved. The only difference between the two cases is how long the
consumer waits before fetching:

| case | consumer fetch delay | consumer leg | bytes pulled |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| control | 5 s (inside the park) | 0.30 s | 580,962,816 |
| late | 65 s (past the park) | 38.31 s | 0 |

Producer log for the late case:

```
P2P <producer-ip>:7777: unbound store kv_request_id=park-late-39 timed out
after 60s without a fetch - failing 1 job(s)
```

### Why this fires in practice

The 60 s clock does not start when prefill completes - it starts at the
producer's FIRST stored chunk. `_build_store_jobs` iterates
`scheduler_output.num_scheduled_tokens` (in-flight requests), `complete_store`
cascades each finished store job to the secondary tiers every step, and
`_reap_unbound_stores` keys off `batches[0].submitted_at`, the oldest batch,
then pops the whole `kv_request_id`.

Measured on an idle H200 with a 98 K-token producer leg: HTTP returned in
6.7 s, the first batch parked at +1 s, and with no fetch sent the reap fired
at first-park + 60 s rather than completion + 60 s (the two predictions
differ by 6 s in that setup; the log lands on the former).

So the failing condition is not decoder queueing. The real budget is
first-chunk-to-fetch < 60 s, where the fetch only happens after the remaining
prefill, the producer's HTTP return, proxy dispatch, decode admission, and
the decode scheduler's lookup/flush. The producer's own prefill spends the
budget first: 6.7 s of it idle at 98 K tokens, 13.3 s under mild concurrent
load on the same GPU. At real concurrency on long prompts the sum passes
60 s with the decoder never queueing at all. Each occurrence costs a 30 s
stall plus a full prompt recompute, which feeds back into the load that
caused the delay.

Both leg-dispatch orders lose, so this cannot be fixed by the caller:

- dispatch the legs concurrently and the fetch can arrive **before** the
  store, so demand parks and the consumer burns its 30 s deadline. This is
  what llm-d/llm-d-router#2451 fixes on the routing-proxy side, by running
  the prefill leg to completion before dispatching decode
- dispatch them sequentially, as that PR does and as the NIXL path already
  did, and the fetch can arrive **after** the 60 s reap - this issue

A post-reap fetch is also not rejected: the reap adds the id to
`_failed_req_ids`, but the fetch-bind path never consults that set (it feeds
only the consumer-side `lookup()` and dead-session teardown, despite the
reap docstring saying otherwise). The late fetch binds, finds nothing, and
parks silently until the consumer's 30 s deadline.

### Steps to reproduce

Two instances, `PF` = producer, `DE` = consumer, both with the tiering spec
and a `p2p` secondary tier.

```sh
M=<model>; ID=park-$$
PROMPT=$(awk 'BEGIN{p="unique-'$ID' ";for(i=0;i<900;i++) p=p "alpha bravo charlie delta echo ";print p}')

# producer leg: stores KV under ID, parks it (no peer has fetched yet)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'producer http=%{http_code} t=%{time_total}\n' \
  -X POST "http://$PF:8000/v1/completions" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$M\",\"prompt\":\"$PROMPT\",\"max_tokens\":1,\"temperature\":0,\"kv_transfer_params\":{\"remote_decoder\":{\"kv_request_id\":\"$ID\"}}}"

sleep 65     # 5 reproduces the working control

curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'consumer http=%{http_code} t=%{time_total}\n' \
  -X POST "http://$DE:8200/v1/completions" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$M\",\"prompt\":\"$PROMPT\",\"max_tokens\":4,\"temperature\":0,\"kv_transfer_params\":{\"remote_prefiller\":{\"kv_request_id\":\"$ID\",\"remote_host\":\"$PF\",\"remote_port\":7777}}}"

# watch vllm:kv_offload_load_bytes_total on the consumer across the pair
```

With `sleep 5` the consumer pulls the blocks in ~0.3 s. With `sleep 65` it
transfers nothing and returns after ~38 s.

### The NIXL path already solves this

`NixlConnector` faces the same question - how long does P hold blocks that D
has not read yet - and answers it with a renewable lease rather than a fixed
timer:

- `_kv_lease_duration` (`nixl/base_scheduler.py`), default **30 s**,
  configurable via `kv_lease_duration`
- `_heartbeat_interval = _kv_lease_duration // 6`, and D sends periodic
  lease-renewal heartbeats to P for every request it still intends to read
- `decoder_kv_blocks_ttl`, default 480 s, for the client-driven turn-2 case

So NIXL's nominal pin is *shorter* than the tier's 60 s, yet a queued consumer
never loses its blocks: the lease is tied to consumer liveness, and only a
consumer that has actually gone away lets it lapse. The p2p tier has no
equivalent - no renewal, no way for the consumer to signal intent, and no
config knob - so it cannot distinguish "the peer is still queued" from "the
peer will never come".

### Suggested direction

Tie the parked store's lifetime to the consumer's liveness instead of a fixed
interval from store time. A few shapes that would work:

- adopt the NIXL contract: let the consumer renew the parked store the way D
  renews P's lease, so a queued request keeps its KV and a dead one releases
  it promptly
- failing that, let the consumer register intent for a `kv_request_id` before
  it is admitted, so the producer knows a peer is coming
- at minimum make the interval configurable like `kv_lease_duration` is,
  since the right value depends on the deployment's admission latency

Worth surfacing the reap as its own counter either way - today it is only a
warning line, so operators see the consumer's recompute without the producer
side that explains it.

cc @liranschour
